boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Georgia Landing record (October 27, 1862) in Operations in LaFourche District [October 1862], a one-engagement campaign; the live campaign label reads Operations in Lafourche District. The landing at Donaldsonville on October 25-26, the Confederate evacuation to Berwick Bay by October 30 and the gunboat actions of November 1-5 are context. Campaign-wide movements and totals are not assigned to one record. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen force field lists eight Confederate units (approx. 1,392 men) against the Reserve brigade, Department of the Gulf, and the frozen Confederate bound is 1,392; the live field reads 5392 total (US 4000; CS 1392) and NPS says Butler organized a brigade of about 4,000 men. Mouton's return-based table totals 1,392 for both banks, with 594 in the 33d Regiment and 150 in the 2d Louisiana Cavalry. Mouton gives Vincent's information of 2,500 to 3,000 enemy infantry, 250 cavalry and two batteries, an enemy of 1,500 to 1,800 on each bank, and at the close of the day about 2,000 infantry, 100 cavalry and a battery against his own barely 1,000. Irwin says Mouton reported 1,392 and names the outlying La Fourche regiment of 500 and 300 men of the 33d.
claims.rationale: Mouton's 1,392 is a return figure for troops on both banks before the fight; the Union figures are NPS's organization figure and Mouton's estimates for different moments. Irwin repeats Mouton's figure and is not an independent check. None is adopted as a matched opening strength.

claims.value: Mouton says the enemy advanced on both banks in about equal force, so he held positions on both sides of the bayou; NPS says his force was divided, generally without means of concentrating. Irwin describes narrow standing room along the bayous and low, heavily wooded ground crossed by deep ditches, where positions and numbers were hard to make out. Mouton says the enemy crossed troops by pontoon bridge to the right bank.
claims.rationale: Ground described by an interested report, a history and a summary; no map verification. The division across the bayou was Mouton's response to the advance, so the phase is left unresolved.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 315 total (US 86; CS 229), and the live field agrees. Mouton reports 5 killed, 8 wounded and 186 missing and estimates the enemy's loss at 250 to 300 on a paroled officer's information. Irwin repeats Mouton's 199 and says Weitzel claimed 208 prisoners and gave his own loss as 18 killed and 74 wounded, with 5 missing in the nominal lists, 97 in all.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. Richard B. Irwin's History of the Nineteenth Army Corps (Putnam's, 1892), already registered for the Red River pass, is an interested Union history by the corps' later assistant adjutant-general. Its Georgia Landing passage gives Mouton's figures from his report, so it is not independent of it. Mouton's November 4, 1862 report (Official Records Series I, Volume XV, a shared container) is one interested Confederate family. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
